summary: A Best Current Practice document that gives implementation recommendations for SMTP mail transfer agents so they can better reduce the impact of spam, for example by tightening how mail is relayed. It asks for discussion and suggestions for improvement.

plainLanguage.summary: This document tells mail server operators what their server should be able to do to limit spam. The main item is refusing to relay mail for people who are not their customers, because that is what spammers use to hide. The rest is about keeping records, so that a spammer who does get through can still be found.

subtitle: A Best Current Practice list of the checks a mail server should make to reduce the damage from spam.

tldr.problem: Unsolicited bulk email costs receivers time and storage, costs internet service providers disk and money, and is usually sent through somebody else's mail server without permission, which makes the spammers hard to find.
tldr.mechanism: The document lists what a mail transfer agent should be able to do: refuse to relay for strangers, record where each message came from, keep logs of its anti-spam decisions, refuse mail from named hosts and addresses, limit the rate at which it accepts mail, and pick reply codes that do not bounce legitimate mail.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2505 is a Best Current Practice and asks for discussion and suggestions for improvement. It says plainly that these rules alone will not stop spam, and that the final answer may well be social, political or legal rather than technical.

today: RFC 2505 is a Best Current Practice and has not been obsoleted. The document asks for discussion and suggestions for improvement, and says plainly that it is not the final answer to spam: it works only if enough mail servers apply it, and the ultimate solution may well be social, political or legal rather than technical.

sections.title: The Problem and the Scope
sections.content:
This memo is a Best Current Practice RFC and is meant as a guideline for SMTP MTA implementors to make their products more capable of preventing and handling spam. An intended side effect is to suggest to the system administrator and postmaster community which anti-spam controls an SMTP MTA is expected to have. It is not generally intended as a description of how to operate an MTA, which controls to turn and how to configure them.

Mass unsolicited electronic mail has increased considerably during a short period of time. The problem has several components. It is high volume, so people get a lot of such mail in their mailboxes. It is completely blind, with no correlation between the receivers' interests and the mail sent out. It costs real money for the receivers, who pay to transfer the mailbox from their service provider to their computer. It costs real money for the service providers: one 10 Kbyte message sent to 10 000 users with their mailboxes at one host means an unsolicited, unexpected storage of 100 Mbytes, and state of the art disks of 4 Gbyte can take 40 such message floods before they are filled.

Many of the senders of spam are dishonest, hiding behind false return addresses. It is also common practice to make use of third party hosts as relays to get the spam mail sent out. This theft of service is illegal in most, if not all, countries, and because the original sender, the innocent relay and the list of receivers can be in different countries, the legal process of getting damages becomes extremely difficult.

The memo has no intention of being the final solution. If enough MTAs implemented enough of the rules described, especially the non-relay rules, the spammers would be out in the open where they could be dealt with. But the non-relay rules are not in themselves enough to stop spam: even if 99 percent of MTAs implemented them from day one, spammers would find the remaining 1 percent, or would switch to connecting directly to each recipient host.
sections.plainLanguage: Spam costs everybody money: receivers pay for the time to download it, and providers pay for the disk it fills. Spammers usually send it through a server that belongs to someone else, so tracking them down is hard. Stopping that relay use is the main thing this document asks for.

sections.title: The List of Recommendations
sections.content:
The document first gives a brief list of recommendations and then discusses each one. It also gives recommendations on things not to do, which may seem natural in the spam fight and might work so far but could wreak havoc on internet mail.

The MTA MUST be able to restrict unauthorized use as a mail relay, MUST be able to provide Received lines with enough information to make it possible to trace the mail path despite spammers using forged host names in HELO statements, and MUST be able to provide local log information that makes it possible to trace the event afterwards. It SHOULD be able to log all occurrences of anti-relay and anti-spam actions, and SHOULD be able to refuse mail from a host or a group of hosts.

It MUST NOT refuse MAIL From: <> and MUST NOT refuse MAIL From: <user@my.local.dom.ain>. It SHOULD be able to refuse mail from a specific MAIL From user or an entire MAIL From domain, SHOULD be able to limit the rate of mail flow, SHOULD be able to verify the MAIL From domain, SHOULD be able to verify the local part in outgoing mail, SHOULD be able to control the SMTP VRFY, EXPN and ETRN commands, and MUST be able to be configured to provide different return codes for different rules.

The interpretation that should apply to all these recommendations is flexibility. However well the anti-spam rules are designed today, spammers will find ways around them, and a well designed MTA should be flexible enough to meet those new threats. String matching on domain and host names MUST NOT be case sensitive, and the document suggests that local part comparisons be case insensitive too.
sections.plainLanguage: The list has thirteen items. Four are absolute requirements, the rest are things a server should be able to do. Two things are forbidden outright: turning away the empty sender address that error messages use, and turning away mail that claims to come from a local user, because both would break ordinary mail.

sections.title: Restricting Unauthorized Mail Relay
sections.content:
Unauthorized usage of a host as a mail relay means theft of the relay's resources and puts the relay owner's reputation at risk. It also makes it impossible to filter out or block spam without at the same time blocking legitimate mail, so the MTA MUST be able to control or refuse such relay usage.

An SMTP session has four elements, each with a different degree of trust: HELO Hostname, easily and often forged; MAIL From, easily and often forged; RCPT To, correct or at least intended; and the SMTP caller host, whose source IP address is good and whose FQDN may be good. Since the first two are so easily forged, they cannot be depended on at all to authorize relay usage.

The MTA MUST instead be able to authorize relay usage based on a combination of the RCPT To address, the SMTP caller FQDN, and the SMTP caller IP address. The suggested algorithm is: if RCPT To is one of our domains, local or a domain that we accept to forward to as an alternate MX, then accept to relay; if the SMTP caller is authorized, by either its source IP or its FQDN depending on whether the DNS is trusted, then accept to relay; else refuse to relay. When doing the first test, all kinds of SMTP source routing must be removed or at least taken into account. The configuration MUST support wild cards for FQDNs and classful IP addresses and SHOULD support address and mask notation for classless IP addresses, and the decision data SHOULD be allowed to contain regular expressions.
sections.plainLanguage: The two things a sender writes about itself can be faked, so they cannot decide whether to relay. The decision rests on who is sending, seen as an IP address or a name, and on whether the mail is addressed to a domain this server handles.

sections.title: Keeping the Trail
sections.content:
The MTA MUST prepend a Received line in the mail, as described in RFC 822 and required in RFC 1123, and that line MUST contain enough information to make it possible to trace the mail path back to the sender. It MUST contain the IP address of the caller and the date and time. It SHOULD contain the FQDN corresponding to the caller's IP address, the argument given in the HELO statement, and authentication information if an authenticated connection was used.

Organizations with a policy of hiding their internal network structure must still be allowed to do so. They usually make their internal MTAs prepend Received lines with a very limited amount of information, or none at all, and send mail out through a firewall or gateway that may remove all the internal Received lines before prepending its own. In that case the information provided in their outgoing mail is REQUIRED to be sufficient for them to perform any necessary traces. For incoming mail the Received lines MUST be kept intact. Generally a gateway SHOULD NOT change or delete Received lines unless it is a security requirement, because changing their content most often destroys information needed to make a message traceable.

The MTA MUST also be able to provide enough local log information to make it possible to trace the event, and SHOULD be able to log all anti-relay and anti-spam actions. The log entries SHOULD contain at least time information, refusal information explaining why the request was refused, the RCPT To addresses, the offending host's IP address, the offending host's FQDN hostname, and other relevant information from the SMTP dialogue. Logging more events opens the possibility of denial of service attacks by filling logs, so the size of the log files increases during attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: Every server that handles a message should write down where it came from, both in the message itself and in its own logs. Those records are what let an internet provider find the sender of a spam message after the fact, and they are the reason the recommendation is as strict as it is.

sections.title: Choosing the Right SMTP Reply Code
sections.content:
SMTP has several classes of return codes. A 5xx is a permanent negative completion reply, a fatal error, and results in the mail transfer being terminated and the mail returned to the sender. A 4xx is a transient negative completion reply, a temporary error, and results in the mail transfer being put back on queue with a new attempt made later. A 2xx is a positive completion reply and indicates that the MTA has taken responsibility for delivering the mail.

The document suggests 4xx as the return code for most cases. Since that is a non-fatal error, the mail gets re-queued at the sender and there is time to discover and correct configuration errors rather than have mail bounce. A 4xx response also makes the spammer's host re-queue the mail, and if it really is his own host, filling its disks with his own spam is probably a good thing. If someone else is being used as the relay host, all that queued mail is strong evidence that something bad is going on at that relay host.

However, 4xx replies may have unexpected interaction with MX records. If the receiving domain has several MX records and the lowest preference host refuses with a 451 response code, the sending host may choose, and often will, use the next host on the list. If that host does not have the same refuse list it will accept the mail, only to find that the final host still refuses it.

Finally, it has been suggested that one may use a 2xx return code and nevertheless decide not to forward or receive the message, storing it elsewhere. This clearly violates the intent of RFC 821 and should not be done without careful consideration. Instead of blindly dropping the mail, one could re-queue it and manually or automatically inspect whether it is spam or legitimate mail.
sections.plainLanguage: When a server turns a message away it has to say how serious that is. A temporary code puts the message back in the sender's queue to try again later; a permanent code bounces it. The document leans towards the temporary code, so that a mistake in the configuration delays mail instead of losing it.

sections.title: Refusing by Address, and What Not to Refuse
sections.content:
The fight against spammers must never be done in a way that violates existing email standards. Since spammers often forge MAIL From addresses it is tempting to put general restrictions on that, especially for some obvious addresses, but this may wreak more havoc on the mail community than spam does. When there is a need to refuse mail from a particular host or site, the recommendation is to use other methods, such as refusing based on the caller's address or name, regardless of what MAIL From was used.

The MTA MUST NOT refuse to receive MAIL From: <>. That address is used in error messages from the mail system itself, for instance when a legitimate mail relay forwards an error message back to the user, and refusing such mail means users may not be notified of errors in their outgoing mail. The MTA MAY however throttle down the TCP connection if there is more than one RCPT To, which slows down spammers using MAIL From: <>.

The MTA MUST NOT refuse MAIL From: <user@my.local.dom.ain>, where the domain names are those treated as local and delivered locally. Restricting it would do away with at least two legitimate usages: aliases, where a forward file sends mail to another address that comes back, and mailing lists, because RFC 1123 requires that the MAIL From for mail from a mailing list reflect the owner of the list rather than the individual sender, and the list owner may be in a different domain from the list host.

The MTA SHOULD be able to refuse mail from a specific MAIL From user or an entire MAIL From domain. Such rules are easily overcome by spammers changing MAIL From every so often, but the ability to block a certain user or domain is quite helpful while an attack has just been discovered and is ongoing. The MTA SHOULD also provide tools to control the rate at which mail is sent or received, SHOULD control who may issue the VRFY and EXPN commands, with the default VRFY response being 252 Argument not checked and the default for EXPN being off, and SHOULD control who may issue the ETRN command, whose default should be off.
sections.plainLanguage: Some obvious-looking rules would break ordinary mail. The empty sender address is how error messages are sent, and a local sender address is used by aliases and mailing lists, so neither may be turned away. Refusing by address is still useful, but it is a tool for handling an attack that is happening now, not a lasting solution.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The increase of spam raises several security issues which puts the entire internet mail community at risk. People may fail to find important mail in their flooded mailboxes, or delete it while cleaning up. ISPs get overloaded mailbox hosts and filled disks, and in fact mail servers have crashed from too much mail. While disks are inaccessible, important mail may be delayed or lost. Hosts used as unauthorized mail relays become overloaded. The fight against spammers includes blocking their hosts, but there is a great risk that mail relay hosts are blocked too, even though they are also victims, and in the long run this may cause internet mail service to deteriorate. The common use of forged MAIL From and From addresses puts the blame on innocent persons, hosts and organizations, which is bad for reputations and may affect business relations.

Several of the methods described in this document increase the load on the support systems of the email system itself, such as DNS, logging, databases with lists of local users and authentication mechanisms, and therefore increase the risk of a denial of service attack by sending spam to a site. The functionality of the support systems during high load should be carefully studied before implementing the methods described. A mail server MUST NOT respond with a permanent failure, 5xx, if there is a temporary problem with one of its support systems.
sections.plainLanguage: Every one of these checks costs something: more DNS lookups, bigger log files, more work for the database of local users. During a spam flood that extra work can itself become the outage, so a server must not report a permanent failure just because one of its helpers is temporarily broken.
